chapter.title: Introduction
chapter.para: This is the manual for the &trelby; screenwriting software. This version of the manual corresponds to version &trelby.version; of the software.

sect1.title: Basic concepts
sect1.para: If you don't know anything about writing a screenplay, get a copy of a book such as David Trottier's "The Screenwriter's Bible". This manual will not cover the same ground, but focuses on concepts specific to &trelby;.
&trelby; divides a screenplay into a long list of elements, each with a specific element style. The available element styles are:

listitem.para: Scene header. Example: "INT. MOTEL ROOM - NIGHT".
Describes action. Example: "John grabs the gun from the desk."
A speaking character's name. Example: "HARRY".
Speech. Example: "You could do that, sure. On the other hand, if you want to live beyond the next minute or so, you might want to rethink your approach."
Describes how the actor should say the following dialogue. Example: "(serious)".
Describes a non-standard transition between scenes. Example: "DISSOLVE TO:".
Describes an in-scene shot. Example: "THE NECKLACE".
Defines an act (typically used in teleplays). Example: "ACT ONE" or "TEASER".

chapter.title: Basic usage
chapter.para: This chapter discusses basic usage of &trelby;.

sect1.title: Main window
sect1.para: The main window has the following parts in it in top-to-bottom order, after the standard menu bar:

listitem.para: Each script gets its own tab, with the tab's name being the filename of each script. You can click on each tab to change the active script to that one, or the X at the end of each tab to close that tab.
After tabs is a column showing the current element's style, a column showing what the Enter/Tab keys would do, and a column showing the current/total page number.
This is where the actual script is shown and edited.

sect2.title: Moving around
sect2.para: The usual movement keys are available: Up/Down/Left/Right to move around, Home/End to move to start/end of line, Page Up/Page Down to move up/down one page (actually one screenful), and CTRL + Home/End to move to start/end of script.
CTRL + Up/Down moves one scene up or down.

sect2.title: Deleting elements
sect2.para: The Delete and Backspace keys delete text one character at a time. They also join elements to one another if pressed at, respectively, at the end or at the start of an element. The joined element will always have the style of the preceding element.

sect2.title: Adding elements and changing their style
sect2.para: The Enter key will always create a new element. If the cursor is at the end of an element, the new element will be an empty one, otherwise the current element is split at the cursor position.
The Tab key will create a new element if the cursor is at the end of an element, otherwise it will switch the current element's style. Shift + Tab will always switch the element's style.

What kind of element Enter/Tab/Shift + Tab will create/switch to is dependent on the current style of the element, and is configurable by the user (see ). These values for Enter/Tab are always shown to the right of the tab-bar.

Other ways to change an element's style are right-clicking with the mouse which will show a menu where you can change the element's style, or pressing a short-cut key for each element style. Note that if you have selected text belonging to multiple elements, all of those elements' types will be changed.
Shift + Enter or CTRL + Enter will insert a forced linebreak.

sect2.title: Selecting text
sect2.para: When selecting text, one end of the selection is always fixed and the other one moves around with the cursor. You can select text by clicking and dragging with the mouse (right-click unselects), or by pressing CTRL + Space which sets the fixed point of the selection at current position and then moving around, or by pressing some movement key together with Shift (e.g. Shift + Up).
You can select the current scene with CTRL + A.
After you've selected the desired text, you can use the cut/copy/paste commands to move text around, delete it, etc. You can also press Del or Backspace to simply delete it.
You can unselect the selected text by pressing Esc., or simply clicking the mouse on the screen.

sect2.title: Auto-completion
sect2.para: Auto-completion saves typing in scene / character / transition / shot elements by showing a list of other elements from the script that match the text in the current element. For example, if you've written the characters "MO" in a new character element, you'll see a list of all character elements that start with "MO" and if you want, you can select one of them and that text will complete the current element.
The auto-completion list only appears after you've written at least one character. If you want to see a list of all possible choices, write a single character and delete it.

You can move around in the list with the Up/Down/Page up/Page down keys. Pressing Enter will complete the text and start a new element, while pressing End will complete the text but will not start a new element. Pressing ESC will make the list go away.

sect2.title: Miscellaneous
sect2.para: When inserting a new empty parenthetical element, "()" will automatically be added to it and the cursor positioned in the middle. Likewise, when switching a parenthetical element to something else, if it only contains "()", it will be replaced by "" (empty). If you write a "(" in an empty dialogue or character element if will switch to a parenthetical element. If you press Enter or Tab at the ending ")" to start a new element, the ")" will stay in the parenthetical.
If you write "EXT." or "INT." (case doesn't matter) at the start of any element, it will switch to a scene element automatically.

chapter.title: View modes
chapter.para: This chapter describes the different view modes available. You can toggle between them using the View-menu or by keyboard shortcuts.

sect1.title: Continuous
sect1.para: In 'Continuous' mode, the text area consists of an empty background with the script's text drawn on top. This text includes only actual script contents, so page headers, CONTINUED/(MORE) and other automatically added texts are not shown at all. Page breaks, if enabled, are shown as a horizontal line (see ).
Reasons you might want to use this mode:

listitem.para: You want to see only actual words you've written, and not be distracted by page-break related formatting.
Page breaks do not take space, so more lines fit onto the screen.
It's the fastest view mode.

sect1.title: Page
sect1.para: 'Page' mode shows an almost exact representation of the page as it would appear when printed. Page borders, margins, headers, CONTINUED/(MORE) and so on are all shown at their correct places, and page breaks are updated as you type.
Ways in which the display in this mode can differ from the printed output:

listitem.para: If you have scene continueds enabled, they will always show as plain "CONTINUED:" on top of the page, whereas in the PDF output, they will be "CONTINUED: (n)" if needed (see ).

sect1.title: Side by side
sect1.para: 'Side by side' mode shows multiple pages side by side, as many as fit on your screen. You need to use a high resolution display and/or small fonts in order to fit more than one page on the screen at a time. Otherwise this mode is the same as the 'Page' mode.
Note that this mode also assumes that the entire pages fit vertically on the screen, so Page up/down commands behave somewhat differently.

chapter.title: Other commands
chapter.para: This chapter describes commands not discussed elsewhere.

sect1.title: File/New screenplay,Open,Save,Save as,Close
sect1.para: These do what you'd expect them to do.

sect1.title: File/New from template, Script/Change format
sect1.para: Besides screenplays, &trelby; can lay a script out as a multi-camera sitcom, a stage play, an audio drama or a comic. File/New from template starts a new script in one of these formats, and Script/Change format switches the current script to another one.
A format uses the usual element types, but lays them out its own way and may call them something else, in the toolbar, the right-click menu and the status bar:

listitem.para: Multi-camera sitcom: action in capitals, dialogue double-spaced, scene headings underlined, and each scene and act on a new page.
Stage play: the dialogue across the page under the speaker's name, and stage directions (Action) indented and in italics. Act breaks are acts, and Shot isn't used.
Audio drama: Shot is for sound effects and Transition for music cues, both in capitals and underlined, and Action is for descriptions.

Comic: Scene headings are the comic's pages (PAGE ONE), Shot its panels (PANEL 1), Action describes a panel, Dialogue is for balloons, and act breaks are chapters. Write captions and sound effects as speeches, with CAPTION or SFX as the character. Transition isn't used.

sect1.para: A format's layout is ordinary script settings (see ), so you can change it afterwards like any others. Changing the format replaces the element styles and the page break settings with the new format's, and clears the undo history; the paper, margins, fonts and the rest are kept.

sect1.title: File/Revert
sect1.para: Replaces the open script with the last version of it saved to disk.

sect1.title: File/Export/Watermarked PDF
sect1.para: This allows you to generate multiple watermarked PDFs to distribute to multiple people. Watermarks are handy when you want to let your readers know overtly that the script is meant only for their viewing, and is not to be distributed.

Enter details like directory, filename prefix, and watermark font size. You can have two lines of watermarks per file, and the first line is common in all files. The second line for each file is provided as a list under the "Watermarks" entry box.
The watermark in the PDF is applied as slanted text, in light grey color, as part of the background of the page. The watermark is applied on every page.
A unique ID is also saved in the 'Keywords' metadata of the PDF file, as a second source of identification of a PDF (if it is leaked with only the watermark removed).

sect1.title: Edit/Undo,Redo
sect1.para: Every edit operation you do to the script is recorded and can be undone/redone. There is a limit to the amount of memory that &trelby; will use to store undo history, and different edit operations take different amounts of memory (adding a single new character takes very little memory, whereas doing a global Find&Replace can take a lot of memory), but in normal usage you should be able to undo hundreds, or even thousands, of edit operations.
There are a few occasions when undo history is otherwise trimmed that you should be aware of:

listitem.para: Applying new script-specific settings clears all undo history.

If you do a new edit operation while you are in the middle of the undo history (i.e., you have done one or more undo operations without having done follow-up redo operations to restore all your previously made changes), all recorded undo history after the current point in it will be discarded.

sect1.title: Edit/Cut,Copy,Paste
sect1.para: Cut, copy and paste work pretty much the same way as in every other program. Note that these commands use &trelby;'s internal clipboard so can't be used for copying text to/from other programs. For that, see below.

sect1.title: Edit/Copy/paste, system
sect1.para: These copy/paste text to the system wide clipboard so can be used for communicating with other programs. Note that if you copy text to the clipboard from &trelby;, you must keep &trelby; open until you've pasted the text to the destination program.
There's two variants of the copy command: formatted and unformatted. Which one you want to use depends on what you're trying to do. Best to try out both and see which one works better.

sect1.title: Edit/Select scene
sect1.para: Select all the text of the current scene.

sect1.title: Edit/Select all
sect1.para: Select all the text in the entire script.

sect1.title: Edit/Goto page
sect1.para: This opens a dialog allowing you to type in a page number to jump to. The Enter/Escape keys can be used as shortcuts for the OK/Cancel buttons.

sect1.title: Edit/Goto scene
sect1.para: This opens a dialog allowing you to type in a scene number to jump to. The Enter/Escape keys can be used as shortcuts for the OK/Cancel buttons.

sect1.title: Edit/Insert non-breaking space
sect1.para: This adds a non-breaking space at the current cursor position. This will ensure that the line will not break at this position when it is being typed/formatted in.

sect1.title: Edit/Find & Replace
sect1.para: This opens a dialog allowing you to search for and possibly replace text. Usually it operates on all element styles, but if you press the "More" button, you can select the element styles it operates on, which is useful when renaming a character and so on.
Pressing Enter while the cursor is in either text box is equivalent to pressing the 'Find next' button. The Esc key will close the dialog.

If you're doing partial replacing, i.e. replacing some, but not all, occurrences of 'foo' with 'bar', the efficient way to do that is to press Tab until the focus is on the 'Find next' button, and then use the 'F' (Find next) and 'R' (Replace) keys on the keyboard. Press 'F' whenever you don't want to replace that occurrence, and 'R' when you do want to replace it.

sect1.title: Edit/Remove elements
sect1.para: 'Remove elements' opens a dialog allowing you to select one or more element styles to completely remove from the script.
You can use this if you want a version of the script with only the dialog, only the action, or only the scene headers, or whatever else you can come up with.

sect1.title: Edit/Add note
sect1.para: This adds a note to the paragraph the cursor is in, and shows it in the notes sidebar (see View/Notes) for you to write. Notes are for reminders to yourself, or the notes you get from producers and readers. Example: "Should Bobby shoot first?". They're never printed. The shortcut is Alt+N, and it's also in the script's right-click menu.

sect1.title: Edit/Alternates
sect1.para: An element can keep alternates: other versions of its text, such as a few ways of saying a line of dialogue, of which only one is in the script, printed and exported. The others are kept with the element, out of sight, to switch to later. Any element can have them, but they're mostly for dialogue and parentheticals.

'Add as alternate' keeps the element's current text as an alternate; then rewrite the element, and both versions are kept. 'Next alternate' (Alt+Right) and 'Previous alternate' (Alt+Left) put the next or previous version in the script in place of the current one, which becomes an alternate. An element with alternates has a small badge left of it on screen, with the number of versions it has; clicking it shows the next one. The 'Alternates' submenu of the script's right-click menu lists the element's versions, the one in the script checked, to switch to.

'Manage alternates' opens a dialog listing all of the element's versions, the one in the script first: select one to see or edit its text below the list (Enter starts a new paragraph, Ctrl+Enter is OK), 'New' adds an empty one, 'Show this one' puts the selected version in the script, 'Move up' and 'Move down' change the order the versions come in when switching, and 'Delete' removes one. To keep only one version, delete the others. Every change is one step to undo.

Alternates stay with their element as the script is edited. Changing the element's type keeps them; splitting it in two leaves them with the first part (unless it's split at its very start); and joining two elements keeps both's alternates. Deleting all of an element's text deletes its alternates too. Final Draft files (.fdx) keep them as Final Draft's own alternates, both ways; other export formats only have the version in the script. AI assistants connected over MCP see and keep them too.

sect1.title: Edit/Settings
sect1.para: This opens the global settings dialog (see ), which also lets you load and save settings files and edit the global spell checker dictionary.
By default, &trelby; loads settings from a file named "default.conf" on startup. See for customizing this.

sect1.title: View/Side panel
sect1.para: This shows or hides the side panel, to the right of the script, which has two tabs: the outline and the notes. Click a tab at the top of the panel to switch between them, and drag the divider to make the panel wider or narrower. The toolbar's button at the far right does the same, and the × at the panel's top right hides it.

sect1.title: View/Outline
sect1.para: This shows the outline in the side panel, or hides the side panel if it's already showing it. The outline lists every scene and act break with its scene number, the page it starts on, and a short summary. The summary is the text of the first note in the scene that isn't resolved, or if there are none, the first action element. The current scene is highlighted as you move around in the script.
Click a scene to jump to it, or press Enter or double-click to jump to it and continue editing there.

To reorder scenes, drag a scene onto the row whose place it should take; the scenes in between shift by one to make room. Dragging past the top or bottom of the list scrolls it, and pressing Escape or releasing the mouse outside the list cancels the move. 'Move up' and 'Move down' (or Ctrl+Up and Ctrl+Down in the list) swap the selected scene with the one before or after it. Either way, everything in the scene moves along with it. Anything before the first scene heading, such as 'FADE IN:', stays where it is. Moving scenes can be undone like any other edit.

An act can be collapsed to hide its scenes, by clicking the arrow left of its act break, pressing Left in the list (Right expands it again), or from the right-click menu, which can also collapse or expand all acts. A collapsed act shows how many scenes it has, and moving it moves the whole act. A scene moved below a collapsed act goes at the end of that act, which is expanded to show it.

sect1.title: View/Notes
sect1.para: This shows the notes in the side panel, or hides the side panel if it's already showing them. The notes sidebar lists the script's notes in script order. Each note shows the page and scene it's in and the start of the paragraph it's about. A note stays with its paragraph as you edit the script, moves with it when you cut and paste it, and is deleted along with all of the paragraph's text. In the script, each note is also shown beside the page, next to its paragraph, with the first few lines of its text (point at it to see all of it). Click it to see it in the notes sidebar, or right-click it to edit it, mark it as resolved, or delete it. Where there isn't room beside the page, as in side by side view, a note icon marks the paragraph instead.

Click a note to go to its paragraph. Double-click it, or press Enter or F2, to edit it; Ctrl+Enter or clicking elsewhere, in the script too, finishes, and Escape cancels. Space marks the note as resolved, or not, and Delete or the × at the note's right deletes it; the right-click menu has these too, and can hide the resolved notes. Every change to the notes can be undone like any other edit.

Notes are saved in the script, exported as notes to Fountain and Final Draft files, and optionally included in HTML exports. Scripts made with older versions of &trelby; had Note elements in the script instead; those become notes on the element before them when the script is opened.

sect1.title: View/Show formatting
sect1.para: This toggles whether formatting information is shown. It consists of blue lines drawn at the right and left margins of each line, plus a red marker indicating the type of the line ending for that line. See fileformat.txt for information about the different marker types.

When using the 'Find errors' command, if you can't figure out what the error is, try switching this on to see if you have two elements where you thought you only had one, or something else that's not obvious in the normal display.
It's also useful for seeing exactly how much space you've got left on a given line.

sect1.title: View/Fullscreen
sect1.para: Changes the display to fullscreen mode, hiding all distractions. To exit fullscreen mode, either press F11 or press the icon at top-left corner.

sect1.title: Script/Script settings
sect1.para: This edits the script format settings (see ): paper size, element formatting, PDF output and so on. The 'Load' and 'Save as' buttons load the settings from, or save them to, a script settings file (.sconf), so you can use the same format for several scripts.

sect1.title: Script/Title pages
sect1.para: 'Title pages' allows you to edit your script's title pages. You can have as many title pages as you want, or none at all.

At the top of the window are add/delete/move/next buttons. 'Add' adds a page, 'Delete' deletes the current page, 'Move' swaps the current page with the next page, and 'Next' changes the view to the next page.
The strings listbox contains all text strings for the current page. Select the text string you want to edit in this listbox, and use the add/delete buttons to add/delete text strings.
On the right side of the listbox is a coarse preview showing the approximate location of text strings on the current page, with the selected text string shown in red.
At the bottom of the window are the settings for the selected text string. There's the text itself (which can consist of multiple lines), the position of it, and its font, size, and style.
The aligment setting has three possible options:

listitem.para: Left-justified. X-Pos setting means the horizontal position of the leftmost edge of the first character.
Centered on the page. X-Pos setting is ignored.
Right-justified. X-Pos setting means the horizontal position of the rightmost edge of the last character.

sect1.para: Finally there's a 'Preview' button that you can use to get an accurate preview of all of the title pages.

sect1.title: Script/Page headers
sect1.para: 'Page headers' allows you to edit your script's headers. Headers are lines that are automatically added to the top of each page of the script, excluding title pages and the first page of the actual script.
Topmost in the window is a setting for how many empty lines you want inserted after your header lines.
After that is a listbox of all the strings in your headers. Select the text string you want to edit in this listbox, and use the add/delete buttons to add/delete text strings.
Below the listbox are the settings for the selected string. You can adjust the string text, style, alignment, line and positioning.

The text is first positioned according to the alignment setting, and then its horizontal starting position is adjusted by the number of characters given in 'X offset'. Note that this parameter can be negative, so for example, if you want your header string to start 2 characters before the left margin, select 'Alignment: Left' and 'X offset: -2'.
The text can contain variables, which are filled in on each page: '${PAGE}' is the page number. 'Insert variable' lists them all; see Script/Page footer for what they are.
The preview on the right shows the top of a page with your headers. 'Apply' applies the new headers to the open script, so you can e.g. see how the page count of the script would change.

sect1.title: Script/Page footer
sect1.para: 'Page footer' sets a line of text printed at the bottom of each page of the script, in the middle of the bottom margin. It has three parts: one aligned to the left margin, one centered and one aligned to the right margin. Leave all three empty for no footer. The footer is not printed on the title pages, and you can leave it off the first page of the script with 'Print on the first page'.

Since the footer is in the margin, it doesn't change how much fits on a page. If the bottom margin is too small for it (see Script/Script settings), it is printed at the very bottom of the page instead.
The parts can contain these variables, which 'Insert variable' puts at the cursor:

listitem.para: '${PAGE}': the page number, e.g. '12' or, for locked pages, '12A'.
'${PAGES}': the number of the last page.
'${TITLE}': the title from the title page.
'${AUTHOR}': the author from the title page, or if it has none, the names below the "by" of the byline.
'${DRAFT}': the draft string from the title page, on one line, e.g. 'Second Draft, May 3, 2026'.
'${DRAFTDATE}': the line of the draft string with the date in it, e.g. 'May 3, 2026'.

sect1.para: The title page values come from the strings of that kind in Script/Title pages, so changing them there changes the footer too. The same variables work in the page headers.

sect1.title: Script/Locations
sect1.para: This dialog allows you to define what scenes are part of the same location (see ). The top listbox shows locations, separated by lines of "-----------", while the bottom listbox shows scenes not part of a user-specified location. In the middle are 'Add' and 'Delete' buttons for moving scenes between the two listboxes. The bottom listbox allows you to select many scenes at once.

An example of how to use this dialog: select the scenes "INT. MOTEL ROOM - DAY", "INT. MOTEL ROOM - DAY - LATER" and "INT. MOTEL ROOM - NIGHT" in the bottom listbox, then click 'Add' which adds those three into a single location in the top listbox. Then, if you want to add more scenes to the same location, make sure one of the scenes for the location is selected in the top listbox, select the new scenes you want to add in the bottom listbox, and click 'Add'. If you want to add scenes to a new location, select one of the "-----------" lines in the top listbox as the destination before clicking 'Add'.

sect1.title: Script/Auto-completion
sect1.para: Here you can define items to be added to the auto-completion lists for Scene, Character and Transition elements, and optionally disable auto-completion for any one of them.

Transition auto-completes are pretty generic so by default there are a few of them here, but the Scene and Character lists are empty. The main use for them are TV shows, where you have a recurring cast of characters and locations, and it's nice to have them always available, even if they haven't yet been used in the current episode's script.

sect1.title: Script/Script dictionary
sect1.para: This opens a dialog allowing you to edit the script-specific spell checker dictionary. Insert new words by entering them on separate lines, or delete existing words by deleting the lines they are on.

sect1.title: Production/Revisions
sect1.para: The Production menu has what's used once a script is in production: revisions, scene numbers, and locking scenes and pages.

Once a script is in production, each round of changes is a revision, named after the color of the paper its pages are printed on: White (the original), Blue, Pink, Yellow, Green, Goldenrod, Buff, Salmon, Cherry, then Double White, Double Blue, and so on.

'Revision mode' turns marking changes on or off. While it's on, the words you change are marked with the current revision: they're highlighted in its color on screen, and their lines get a revision mark (*) in the right margin, on screen and when printed. Deleting text marks the line it was deleted from. Marks stay with their text as it's edited and rewrapped, and are saved with the script. The status bar shows the current revision while revision mode is on. Turning it on before any revision has been started starts the first one, Blue, dated today. Turning it on also locks the pages and the scene numbers (see below), if they aren't locked yet, as production scripts are locked before their first revision; undo unlocks them again.

'Revision settings' chooses the current revision and its date, the revision mark, whether each revised page shows its revision above its header (for example "Blue Rev. 10/17/26"; a page's revision is the latest one marked on it), whether only the current revision's changes get revision marks, and whether turning revision mode on locks the pages and scene numbers (on by default; turn it off to mark changes on a script that isn't in production). Page headers can also show the page's revision with the ${REVISION} variable. Start a new revision by choosing the next color here; the older marks keep their colors.

'Export revised pages' exports a PDF of only the pages with changes marked with the current revision, for handing out as replacement pages; lock the pages first (Production/Lock pages) so that the other pages keep their numbers. 'Clear revision marks' removes all the marks, making every page White again.
Exporting to Final Draft (FDX) keeps the revision marks, as Final Draft revision sets, and the scene numbers when they're locked or printed. Importing an FDX file reads its revision marks back.

sect1.title: Production/Show scene numbers
sect1.para: 'Show scene numbers' puts each scene's number to the left and right of its scene heading, on screen and in exports. This is usually only done once a script is in production, so it's off for new scripts. It's the same setting as 'Include scene numbers' in the script's Formatting settings.

sect1.title: Production/Lock scene numbers
sect1.para: 'Lock scene numbers' makes every scene keep the number it has now. After that, a scene added after scene 12 becomes 12A (then 12B, ...), one added before scene 1 becomes A1, deleting a scene leaves an omitted scene in its place (see below) instead of renumbering the scenes after it, and a scene that is moved, in the outline or by cutting and pasting it, keeps its number. Unchecking it removes the locks and numbers the scenes 1, 2, 3, ... again. The numbers are shown in the outline and the scene report, and on the pages if 'Show scene numbers' is on.

sect1.title: Production/Omit scene
sect1.para: 'Omit scene' replaces the scene the cursor is in with a scene heading reading OMITTED, which keeps the scene's number, as shooting scripts do with cut scenes. Once the scene numbers are locked, deleting a whole scene (selecting it and deleting or cutting it) does this by itself. Pasting a cut scene back gives it its number back, and its OMITTED heading goes away. Deleting an OMITTED heading removes the number for good.

sect1.title: Production/Lock pages
sect1.para: 'Lock pages' locks every page to start where it starts now, with its current page number. After that, adding text creates A-pages (12A, 12B, ...) instead of moving text onto later pages, and removing text leaves gaps instead of pulling text back. This is normally done once a script goes into production. Unchecking it removes the locks and repaginates the script normally.

sect1.title: Production/Breakdown
sect1.para: A breakdown lists what each scene needs to be shot: its cast, extras, stunts, vehicles, props, special and visual effects, wardrobe, makeup and hair, animals, music, sound, set dressing and special equipment. It's what scheduling and budgeting start from.

To tag something, select it in the script (or just put the mouse on a single word), right-click, and pick its category under 'Tag as'. The tagged text is highlighted in the category's color wherever it appears in that paragraph, and the tag stays with the paragraph as the script is edited. Right-clicking tagged text offers to remove the tag. 'Highlight breakdown tags' turns the highlighting on and off.

'Breakdown' opens the side panel's Breakdown tab, which shows what the scene at the cursor needs, by category, or everything in the whole script with how many scenes each is in. The speaking characters are counted as cast without being tagged (their names are dimmed, with "speaks"); the panel's right-click menu turns this off. The + button adds something the scene needs that its text doesn't mention, such as a rain machine. Double-clicking an element goes to it (in the whole script, to the next scene it's in), and its right-click menu renames it, moves it to another category, or removes it from the scene or the whole script. Things tagged with the same category and name are the same element, so renaming one renames it everywhere; to make two names one element, rename one to the other.

Reports/Breakdown report shows a breakdown sheet for each scene (its number, heading, page, length in eighths of a page, and what it needs) and the list of every element with its scenes. File/Export/Breakdown (CSV) saves the breakdown as a spreadsheet, a row per scene and a column per category, for scheduling software. AI assistants connected over MCP can read the breakdown (get_breakdown) and tag elements.

The tags go to Final Draft and back: File/Export/Final Draft (FDX) writes them for Final Draft's tagger, each in Final Draft's category of the same name (extras are its Background Actors), and importing an FDX file reads its tags back. Final Draft categories that Trelby hasn't got become Miscellaneous, except Mechanical Effects (special effects), Greenery (set dressing) and Animal Wrangler (animals). Things a scene needs that its text doesn't mention are tagged on its whole scene heading in Final Draft, and a whole scene heading tagged there comes back as such.

sect1.title: Tools/Spell checker
sect1.para: Words the spell checker doesn't recognize are underlined with a red wavy line as you write, unless 'Underline misspelled words' is turned off in the Misc settings. The word you're typing isn't underlined until you move on from it. Right-clicking an underlined word shows up to 5 similar words to replace it with, and lets you add it to the global or the script's dictionary.
This spell checks the current script beginning at the current position. If you want to spell check the entire script, be sure to position the cursor at the first line of the script.

If it finds any words it doesn't recognize, it jumps to that position in the script, highlights the word, and opens a dialog window that has a text box for editing the word, and the following 5 buttons:

listitem.para: Replace the word in the script with the (modified) one in the text box. You can also do this by pressing Enter in the text box.
Skip the word for now.
Add the word to the script-specific dictionary.
Add the word to the (super-)global dictionary.

Search for the 5 most similar known words and allow choosing one of them. If selected, that word is put in the text box and you can either edit it further or press 'Replace' at once to replace the word in the script.

Note that this only looks at words with the same two first characters as the misspelled word (mostly for speed reasons). So while it can correct "accommdoate" to "accommodate", it can't correct "cmoputer" to "computer".

sect1.para: After pressing any of the above buttons, the spell checker looks for the next misspelled word. If none are found, it closes the dialog. You can also press the Esc key at any time to close the dialog.
Note that the spell checker currently only supports the English language.

sect1.title: Tools/Check formatting errors
sect1.para: 'Check formatting errors' checks the whole script for formatting errors and lists every one it finds in a dialog, with the page it's on, the element type, what's wrong and the line's text.

Selecting an error in the list shows it in the script behind the dialog. 'Go To' (or double-clicking the error) closes the dialog with the cursor on that error, so you can fix it; 'Close' puts the cursor back where it was. Run the command again after fixing errors to see what's left.
It can detect the following errors:

listitem.para: An empty line, or a parenthetical element containing only ().
A character element that is not followed by a parenthetical or a dialogue element.
A parenthetical element that does not follow a character or a dialogue element.
A dialogue element that does not follow a character or a parenthetical element.

Various error conditions that can only arise from bugs in the program. This includes things like overlong lines, elements that have lines with different element types, invalid characters in the script, etc. You should never find any of these errors, but if you do, you should try to fix them before saving the script, otherwise you might not be able to load it again. You should also notify us about the problem so we can fix it.
The messages for these all say "(BUG)" at the end so they can be identified from normal errors.

sect1.title: Tools/Name database
sect1.para: 'Name database' opens a window allowing you browse and search through a database of more than 200,000 character names, each name being categorized by its nationality and sex.
On the left side of the window is a list of the name categories. The main groups available are nationalities, but there are some other interesting groups, e.g. Shakespeare, Medieval, Flowers etc.

Select the groups you want to search in, either a single one by simply clicking on it, or multiple ones by holding down CTRL and then clicking on multiple items. If you want to go back to the default of having all the groups selected, press the 'Select all' button at the bottom of the list.
On the upper right side of the window are the other search parameters. There's a text box in which you can write the text you want to search for, and two radio button groups.
The first one affects how your search string is used. The string has to match either a) at the start of the name, b) anywhere in the name or c) at the end of the name.
The second one selects whether male/female/both names are included in the search results.
The search is always case-insensitive, and a blank search string matches all names.

After having set all the search parameters, press the 'Search' button, at which point the results list will change to contain only the names matching the search parameters. A count of the matching names is shown at the bottom of the window.
You can select names from the result list and press 'Insert' to insert that name at your script at the current cursor position.

sect1.title: Tools/Character map
sect1.para: 'Character map' opens a window allowing you to insert any character from the supported ISO-8859-1 (i.e. Latin-1) character set into your script.

sect1.title: Tools/Read aloud
sect1.para: 'Read aloud' gives your script a table read: &trelby; reads it aloud from the cursor using your computer's own text-to-speech voices, with a narrator reading the scene headings, action, transitions and shots, and each character speaking their dialogue in a voice of their own. Character names and parentheticals aren't read; the voice tells you who's speaking. The element being read is highlighted, and the cursor follows it.

The voices are given out automatically: the narrator gets the system's default voice, and the characters with the most lines get the other voices first. Where a character's gender can be told from their name (from the name database, or words like "Mrs." or "Waitress"), they get a voice of that gender. As most computers only have two or three voices, characters beyond that share voices, speaking faster or slower to tell them apart.

listitem.para: F5: 'Read from cursor / pause' starts reading at the element the cursor is in, and while reading pauses or resumes. Resuming reads the paused element again from its start.
F6 and Shift+F6: 'Next element' and 'Previous element' skip forward or back.
Shift+F5 or Escape: 'Stop reading'.

sect1.para: Editing the script, or switching to another script, stops the reading.

The voices come from the operating system: on Windows its speech voices (Settings / Time & language / Speech), which need the pyttsx3 package when running &trelby; from source (pip install trelby[speech]); on macOS those of the say command (System Settings / Accessibility / Spoken Content); and on Linux those of espeak-ng, which you may need to install with your package manager.

sect1.title: Tools/Compare scripts
sect1.para: You need two different versions of the same script open to use 'Compare scripts'. Select the older one as the first script and the newer one as the second script. &trelby; then goes through the scripts looking for changes between them and displays the results as a PDF file.

There's a checkbox allowing you to use the same configuration parameters for the scripts you're comparing. This is useful if the scripts differ in in their formatting settings, because in that case practically the entire script would show up as changed.

The PDF file contains only the changed parts of the script. The changes are color coded: Deleted lines are red, added lines are green, non-changed lines (shown for context) are white, and marker lines for single-line changes are yellow. The changed parts are separated by two gray lines.

sect1.title: Help/Commands
sect1.para: 'Commands' opens a window showing all the commands and their current keyboard shortcuts. It also has a menu allowing you to save this as a HTML file if you e.g. want to print it for reference.

sect1.title: Help/Manual
sect1.para: 'Manual' opens this manual you're reading right now.

sect1.title: Help/About
sect1.para: 'About' opens the about screen for &trelby;, showing information such as the version of the program. It also shows a random famous movie quote.

chapter.title: Settings
chapter.para: &trelby; has 4 levels of settings: super-global settings, global settings, script format settings, and script-specific settings.
Super-global settings are the current view mode, window size and position, and the global spell checker dictionary. There can only be one set of these.

Global settings are things like interface colors, keyboard shortcuts, display fonts and other settings that only affect the user interface of the program, not the script output. You can have multiple sets of these and switch between them at will (see ). These settings are platform-dependent, so you can't share these between Windows/Linux machines, and even sharing between different machines on the same platform could be unreliable if you don't have the exact same fonts, PDF viewer applications, etc. on the machines.

Script format settings are things like paper sizes, indendation/line widths/font styles for the different element types, whether to include scene numbers, and so on that directly affect script formatting and output but are not tied to any specific script, in the sense that they can be reused for different scripts with no changes. You can easily save/load these, so you can have ready-made settings for different scenarios. This, and script-specific settings, are completely platform-neutral, guaranteeing the exact same script output whatever platform you use.

Script-specific settings are things that are specific to one particular script, like title pages, header strings, and auto-completion settings, and so can't be reused for different scripts without changes. However, if you want to have a template for these (e.g. your contact information on the title page is always the same, or you're writing several episodes of the same TV show), it's easy: just fill in the information you want, and save the script as "my_template.trel", then when you want to use that as a template, open that file, change what's needed, and save the script under a new name.

sect1.title: Global settings
sect1.para: The global settings dialog is found under Edit/Settings. It has a list of categories on the left, the selected category's settings on the right, and three buttons, Apply, Cancel and OK on the bottom. Apply updates the settings to the ones given in the dialog so you can easily preview your changes without closing the dialog. Note that pressing Cancel after Apply has no effect, it only cancels changes that haven't yet been committed.

The Load and Save as buttons on the bottom left load the dialog's settings from a file, or save them to one. Loaded settings take effect on Apply or OK, like any other change, and from then on changes are saved to that file.

The global spell checker dictionary is edited with the Global dictionary button on the Misc page. Insert new words by entering them on separate lines, or delete existing words by deleting the lines they are on. Dictionary changes are saved as soon as you close its dialog with OK.
The following sections detail the various settings.

sect2.title: Theme
sect2.para: Chooses the colors &trelby; uses on screen: Light, Dark, Parchment, Solarized Light, Solarized Dark, Monokai, Dracula or Nord. Each theme also gives scene headings, character names and other element types their own text colors. 'System default' uses Light or Dark, following the light or dark mode setting of your operating system. Themes only affect the display, the PDF output is always black on white.

You can also make your own themes. A theme is a file ending in .json in the 'themes' folder of the &trelby; settings folder ('Trelby\conf\themes' in your user folder on Windows, '~/.config/trelby/themes' on Linux). Click 'Open themes folder' to open it. The easiest way to start is to pick the theme closest to what you want and click 'Export...', which saves it as a theme file in that folder, named after the file. Edit the file in any text editor, then click 'Reload' to see your theme in the list. Themes are also read when &trelby; starts.
A theme file looks like this (most colors left out):

listitem.para: The name shown in the list. If left out, the file's name is used. It can't be the name of another theme. Your choice of theme is saved by name, so if you remove a theme file, System default is used until it's back.
true if the theme is dark, so that the rest of &trelby; (menus, dialogs and toolbar icons) uses its dark appearance too, false if not.

Each color is either "#rrggbb" in hexadecimal, as in web pages, or [red, green, blue] with values from 0 to 255. These colors are required: text, textHdr (page headers), textBg (the page), workspace (around the pages), pageBorder, pageShadow, selected, cursor, autoCompFg and autoCompBg (the auto-completion list), pagebreak, pagebreakNoAdjust, tabText, tabBorder, tabBarBg and tabNonActiveBg.

These are optional: the text colors of scene, action, character, dialogue, parenthetical, transition, shot, and actBreak, which default to text; and accent and accentText, for the selected item in lists, which go together and default to the operating system's highlight colors; and spellError, the underline of misspelled words, which defaults to red.

sect2.para: A theme file with an error, such as a missing color or a misspelled color name, is skipped, and the Theme page says what is wrong with it.

sect2.title: Display
sect2.para: The topmost listbox allows you to configure what font you want to use for normal, bold, italic, and bold + italic text. Note that you should use the same size font for each one.

sect2.title: Continuous Mode
sect2.para: These settings have an effect only in the 'Continuous' view mode.
The row spacing setting affects how many pixels there are between each row. Changing the screen font on the Display page resets it to suit the new font.

The 'Page break lines to show' setting affects how page breaks are shown. If you select 'None', they are not shown at all. 'Normal', you see solid gray lines in the scripts indicating actual page break positions. 'Normal + unadjusted', you see the solid lines, but you also see a dotted gray line, that shows where the page could have ended, but that the page break position was adjusted backwards to honor the settings in .

This is useful when you've finished your script and you're going through it trying to reduce the page count. If, for example, you have three lines, a Character, a Parenthetical, and a Dialogue element, all one line, and the unadjusted page break line is after the Parenthetical line, and the actual page break line is above the character line, you know that if you can trim just one line from the page, all three lines will then fit on the page instead of being pushed to the next page.

sect2.title: Elements
sect2.para: This is where you configure the interaction parameters for each element style.
At the top is a combo box where you specify what element style you're configuring. All things below that are element-specific settings.

The 'Enter/Tab creates' and 'Tab/Shift+Tab switches to' affect what element is created when Enter or Tab is pressed in this element style, or what element style Tab/Shift+Tab switches the element to. See for more information.

sect2.title: Keyboard
sect2.para: Here you can configure keyboard shortcuts for each command. Note that a few command/keys (Enter, Tab, etc.) can't be changed because they're an integral part of the program's design.

sect2.title: Misc
sect2.para: The default script directory setting allows you to specify the default directory for File/Open dialog on program startup.

'Auto-capitalize sentences', if on, auto-capitalizes sentences as you write them. If it capitalizes something you don't want capitalized, write another letter, and then replace the capitalized letter by a lowercase one.
'Auto-capitalize i -> I', if on, causes solitary 'i' characters in the middle of sentences to be changed to a 'I' character automatically.
'Underline misspelled words', if on, draws a wavy line under words the spell checker doesn't recognize as you write (see Tools/Spell checker).
'When opening a script, start at last saved position' causes the cursor position be restored to the point it was at when the script was saved.

'Recenter screen on scrolling' causes moving around the script using up/down keys to scroll a bit differently: when cursor is at bottom of the screen, and you press down, instead of moving the display down just one line, it will recenter the display on the cursor.
'Typing replaces selected text' causes selected text to be removed and replaced with the character entered whenever a key is pressed and there's an active selection.

'Check script for formatting errors before export or compare', if checked, causes the program to run 'Tools/Check formatting errors' automatically before export/compare operations. This is to avoid printing 100 pages and then finding there's an error on one of them, fixing of which causes repagination of the entire script, and having to print all the 100 pages again.
'Lines to scroll per mouse wheel event' needs no explaining.

sect2.title: PDF
sect2.para: You can specify what application you want to use as your PDF viewer. On Windows, this is usually Adobe Acrobat, and the path is something like "C:\Program Files\Adobe\Acrobat 7.0\Reader\AcroRd32.exe". On Linux, you can also use Adobe Acrobat, path being something like "/usr/local/Adobe/Acrobat7.0/bin/acroread". The Guess button tries to find an installed viewer for you.
You can also specify arguments to give to the PDF viewer program.

sect1.title: Script format settings
sect1.para: Script format settings are found in Script/Script settings. It has the same Apply/Cancel/OK buttons as the global settings dialog.

sect2.title: Elements
sect2.para: This is where you configure the formatting parameters for each element style.
At the top is a combo box where you specify what element style you're configuring. All things below that are element-specific settings.
The Screen/Print areas hold four checkboxes, Caps/Bold/Italic/Underlined, affecting the text style for the element. Screen affects the editing screen, while Print affects PDF output.
The 'Empty lines / 10 before' setting is linespacing before the element, divided by 10. So a value of 10 means normal linespacing, 15 means 1.5 linespacing, 20 is double linespacing, etc.
The 'Empty lines / 10 between' is the same, but for intra-element linespacing, i.e. consecutive lines of the same element have this much space between them.

The Indent and Width settings specify in characters how much the element is indented (i.e. set off from the left margin) and how wide it is. 10 characters (in the default 12-point font) equal one inch.

sect2.title: Formatting
sect2.para: Here you can configure parameters affecting the formatting of the script.

The first two settings affect how many action and dialogue lines there must be left at the end of a page to allow breaking at that position. This only affects elements that are broken in the middle, i.e. if you have a one-line element, the page can always end after that.
The font size specifies the font size to use. 12 is the default, and you should only deviate from this if you have a very good reason.

'Include scene continueds', if enabled, inserts "(CONTINUED)" at the end of each page that has a scene that continues to the next page, and "CONTINUED: (n)" (n = number of CONTINUED pages for current scene, omitted if n = 1) for each page that continues a scene from previous page(s).
'Scene continueds indent' is the number of characters to indent the "(CONTINUED)" text with.

'Include scene numbers' causes scene numbers to be inserted to the left and right of each scene element, on screen and in exports. This is usually only done for scripts in production, so it is off by default. Production/Show scene numbers turns it on and off too.

'Show line numbers' prefixes each line with its line number (starting from 1 at the top of the page). It can be considered a debug option as it has no use in normal operation, but it can be useful if you're trying to figure out printing related problems.

sect2.title: Paper
sect2.para: Here you can configure your output paper size and margins. You can use A4, Letter, or a custom paper size. At the bottom of the page is shown the number of lines that will fit on a page with the given settings.

sect2.title: PDF
sect2.para: Here you can configure parameters affecting the generation of the PDF file for exporting.

'Add table of contents', if on, will cause the PDF file to have a table of contents listing all the scenes. Note that this is not printed, it's just shown in PDF viewer applications allowing one to quickly jump to the selected scene.
'Show table of contents on PDF open', if on, will cause the table of contents to be shown by default when opening the PDF file.

'Show margins' draws a rectangle on each page showing the margin settings. It can be considered a debug option as it has no use in normal operation, but it can be useful if you're trying to figure out printing related problems.

sect2.title: PDF/Fonts
sect2.para: Here you can configure the fonts used in generating the PDF files. Normally they use Courier Prime, a Courier font that comes with Trelby and is also the default font on the screen, so the PDF looks like the script does in Trelby. It is embedded in the PDF files, so they look the same everywhere, and it is strongly recommended to leave things as they are unless you have specific reasons to use other fonts.
So, assuming you have a good enough reason, you can use the TrueType fonts of your choosing. There are four different font settings, one for each font style (Normal / Bold / Italic / Bold-Italic).

Each font setting has two parts: a 'Name' field and a 'File' field. The 'Name' field is the internal Postscript name of the font and is used by the PDF viewer application to recognize the font to use.
The 'File' field is the filename of the TrueType font to use. If you fill in this field, the font file is embedded in the generated PDF files.
Embedding a font will increase the size of the PDF files, and not all fonts allow embedding in their license terms.
When you use the 'Browse' button to locate a font file, the following things happen:

listitem.para: The file is checked to be a valid TrueType font file.
The font's Postscript name is located from the font file and put in the 'Name' field.
The licensing terms of the font are checked and if embedding is not allowed, a warning is printed.

sect2.para: Note that the chosen fonts have to be able to be substituted in place of the normal Courier fonts with no changes to the text layout, i.e., they have to be fixed width fonts with the same size as the Courier fonts are. If this is not the case, you will see characters overlapping each other and other errors in the output.

Also note that random fonts downloaded from the Internet are very often broken in every sense of the word. They have names that violate the Postscript/PDF specifications, they lack essential characters (it is very rare for them to contain anything outside of the ASCII character set), and their quality is bad. So, if you feel you must use something besides the normal Courier fonts, at least use professional fonts made by people who know what they're doing.

Note for Windows users: Microsoft, in their infinite wisdom, have found yet another way to obstruct people from using their computers. When you use the 'Browse' button and navigate to e.g. the 'C:\Windows\Fonts' directory to choose a TrueType font file, the files are listed correctly but you can't select them! One wonders what goes on in those meetings at Microsoft where things like this are decided... "Why would anyone ever want to select a font file from a normal file open dialog?" "Gee Bob, I don't know, maybe we should disallow that so that users aren't confused?" "Good idea Jim, let's do that!".

To work around this bit of brokenness, once you're in the directory containing the font file you want to use, switch the keyboard focus to the filename entry field and type in the first few characters of the filename, after which a completion pop-up should show up from which you can select the correct filename.

sect2.title: Strings
sect2.para: Here you can customize the strings that are automatically added to the script in certain situations:

listitem.para: Added at the end of a page when a scene spans multiple pages.
Added at the start of a page when a scene spans multiple pages.
Added at the end of a dialogue element that spans multiple pages.
Added after the speaker's name at the start of a page when a dialogue element spans multiple pages.

sect1.title: Script-specific settings
sect1.para: Decriptions for these start at .

chapter.title: Import and export
chapter.para: This chapter discusses the import/export support of the program.

sect1.title: Import
sect1.para: Existing screenplays can currently be imported from three file formats: as formatted ASCII text, Final Draft XML (.fdx), Celtx (.celtx), Adobe Story (.astx), Fountain (.fountain) and Fade In Pro (.fadein). The following section documents the format these files should have for optimal import processing.

sect2.title: ASCII Text files
sect2.para: ASCII text files should have the following characteristics:

listitem.para: Each element style should begin at a unique column. An exception is that Scene and Action can begin at the same column.
There should only be one such starting column per element style, i.e. all dialogue should begin at the same column, it shouldn't sometimes start at column 25, sometimes at 27, etc.
No production markings, e.g. scene numbers, page numbers, cast lists, or anything like that.
Elements should be separated by a single empty line.

sect2.para: Below is a short example of the kind of format best recognized by &trelby;.
sect2.screen:
EXT. OCEAN - NIGHT
The package hits the water and is submerged. A few seconds later, a rapidly inflating liferaft appears.
The people land into the water in their parachutes. They dispose of them and swim toward the liferaft.
INT. LIFERAFT - NIGHT
They're all aboard, taking off their clothes. When they're all naked, Sarah gathers the wet clothes, throws them out, and closes the entrance to the tent-like liferaft. The men openly admire Sarah's body, as she opens a storage locker and takes out dry clothes for everyone which they then put on.
KEVIN I know a great way to warm up.
SARAH Sorry, I got over the "older men" thing a while back.
KEVIN Anytime you have a flashback, let me know.
Something starts beeping.

sect2.title: Final Draft XML (.fdx)
sect2.para: Final Draft files saved with version 8 of the program are supported with these contents imported:

listitem.para: Text of the the screenplay elements (Action, Dialog, etc) that Trelby understands.
Script notes in Final Draft are imported as notes.

sect2.para: Note that no formatting settings are imported at all.

sect2.title: Celtx (.celtx)
sect2.para: These files are created by the Celtx program.

listitem.para: Screenplay elements (Action, Dialog, etc) that Trelby understands are imported. Others are converted to 'Action' type.

sect2.para: Note that no formatting settings are imported at all.

sect2.title: Adobe Story (.astx)
sect2.para: These files are created by the Adobe Story editor.

listitem.para: Screenplay elements (Action, Dialog, etc) that Trelby understands are imported. Others are converted to 'Action' type.

sect2.para: Note that no formatting settings are imported at all.

sect2.title: Fountain (.fountain)
sect2.para: Fountain is an open, plaintext screenplay markup language. It is documented at http://fountain.io/syntax.
Almost all of the spec is supported. The below are unsupported:

listitem.para: Emphasis markup (bold, italic, etc) is not supported. When importing, you can choose to retain the syntax, or remove it.
Dual dialogue is imported as a couple of dialogues instead.
Section/Synopsis are imported as notes.
Comments that are part of another element are not recognized. (Standalone comments are imported as notes).
Title pages are imported as action lines. You can also choose not to do this when importing.
Page breaks are not supported (imported as an action line).

sect2.para: Note that no formatting settings are imported at all.

sect2.title: Fade In Pro (.fadein)
sect2.para: These files are created by the Fade In Pro screenwriting program.

listitem.para: Screenplay elements (Action, Dialog, Notes, etc) that Trelby understands are imported. Others are converted to 'Action' type.

sect2.para: Note that no formatting settings are imported at all.

sect1.title: Export
sect1.para: You can export the script in PDF, RTF, Word (.docx), formatted ASCII, HTML, Final Draft XML (.fdx) and Fountain (.fountain) format.

Each has its own entry in the File/Export menu. To print the script, export it as PDF and print that. If you export as a text file, &trelby; will ask whether you want the page markers included or not. If you're planning on importing the script to some other program, you shouldn't include them, otherwise you probably should.

The RTF file produced uses stylesheets, which not all RTF reading programs support, so if you get unexpected output check with something like OpenOffice to see whether the problem is with the file or with the program you tried to use.

The Word file also uses a style for each element type, so it stays easy to edit. Word lays out the pages itself, so its page breaks can differ from &trelby;'s, and it doesn't add (MORE) and (CONT'D) where a speech goes on to the next page. The title pages, page headers and footer are kept, with the page numbers as Word fields, but notes, revision marks and scene numbers are left out.

chapter.title: Reports
chapter.para: This chapter discusses the various report types &trelby; can generate. All the reports are in PDF format so that you can easily view them on your computer, and if necessary also get high-quality printed output.

sect1.title: Script report
sect1.para: The script report is a short, one-page report on general script statistics. It has the following information:

listitem.para: Total line count of the script and line counts for each element type, both in absolute terms and as a percentage of the whole.
Percentage of lines found in interior and exterior scenes (it determines this based solely on whether the scene element starts with INT. or EXT.)
Maximum and average scene lengths in lines.
Maximum and average action element lengths in lines.
Number of different speaking characters.

sect1.title: Location report
sect1.para: The location report is similar to the scene report, but combines scenes taking place at the same location into one entity. If you always use the same scene line to describe a single location, you don't need to do anything special to get a correct location report. If, however, you have e.g. scenes named "INT. MOTEL ROOM - DAY", "INT. MOTEL ROOM - DAY - LATER" and "INT. MOTEL ROOM - NIGHT" and you'd like them to be treated as the same location, see for details on how to do that.

The location report lists the following information for each location: list of scenes for the location (if more than one, each is followed by a percentage showing its part of the total lines of the location), total lines in location, percentage of action lines in location, percentage of the location's total lines of the script's total lines, how many scenes the location has, count of pages that the location appears in, list of pages that the location appears in, and optionally a list of all speaking characters in the location along with the number of lines they speak.

sect1.title: Scene report
sect1.para: The scene report lists the following information for each scene: scene number, scene name, total lines in scene, percentage of action lines in scene, count of pages that the scene appears in, list of pages that the scene appears in, and optionally a list of all speaking characters in the scene along with the number of lines they speak.

sect1.title: Character report
sect1.para: 'Character report' first opens a window allowing you to specify what to include in the generated report. You can select what characters are included, and what kind of information to include for each character:

listitem.para: Total number of speeches, total number of lines, the percentage of all the dialogue lines in the script that this character speaks (i.e. 25% would mean this character has one-fourth of the total dialogue in the script), average number of lines per speech, total words, average number of words per speech and average number of characters per word.
Number of pages this character speaks on, followed by a list of all of those pages.
A list of all the locations this character speaks in, preceded by the number of lines spoken at each location.

sect1.title: Dialogue chart
sect1.para: 'Dialogue chart' first opens a window allowing you to specify what to include in the generated chart. The 'Sorted by:' options select what orderings to include, while the 'Characters < 10 lines' option, if unselected, leaves out all characters that have less than 10 dialogue lines, which is useful for trimming out minor characters from long scripts.
It then generates a chart with one page for each selected ordering and shows that.
The chart has two axes: The horizontal one, with page numbers increasing from left to right, and the vertical one, with characters ordered by the current page's sort criterion from top to bottom.

If a character speaks on a given page, he will have a black bar on that page's position on the chart. The bar's height is scaled according to how many dialogue lines the character has on that page, allowing easy visual identification of long monologues, etc.
Every other line has a light gray background to allow easier visual matching of distant markings to character names.

You can use this chart in many ways. For example, you can at a glance see if one of your side characters disappears for 50 pages in the middle of the script, whether the villain is introduced too late, and so on.

At the top is another graph showing the percentage of action, dialogue, character and "other" lines on each page. This graph is most useful for seeing how the percentage of action lines fluctuates, allowing one to easily see where the major action scenes are, etc.

chapter.title: Troubleshooting
chapter.para: This chapter discusses some common problems you might encounter.

listitem.para: The program usually works perfectly, but sometimes it's so much slower that it's almost unusable.

This happens on certain machines with limited resources. Try stopping all other programs and restarting &trelby; and see if that helps; if so, make it a habit of starting &trelby; first so it can allocate the resources (video memory, mainly) that it needs for fast operation before starting other programs.

appendix.title: File format
appendix.para: The file format used by &trelby; for scripts is open and documented, and third parties are encouraged to add support for the format in their programs and/or write utility programs that use the file format in some way.

For more information, see the file 'fileformat.txt' in the program's installation directory, and read through the sample script file provided. If you still have questions about the file format, feel free to contact us by email.
